constraints.evidence: Slide 14 computes company gross margin against the 75% floor: 76% at beta-average use, 74.1% with Pro accounts at buyer-level use and no cap, 75.7% with the cap. The $0.6M platform cost is counted as cost of revenue (footnote).

Slide 13 sizes the NRR gap at $2.3M a year, i.e. 4 points on $57.6M. It derives 26% Pro migration from the $893 premium per account, states what is held constant, and nets mobile churn separately on slide 17.

Slides 11 and 14 give inference cost at $0.009: $61.20 for buyers (41% of $149), $130.50 for the top decile, $32.40 for the mean. The 58% usage concentration is stated. The Pro margin headline is built from these costs. The document does not give the add-on's product margin against the 75% floor.

The $0.6M platform cost is included in the slide 14 company gross margin (Copilot cost $1.86M = inference + $0.6M). It is not netted in the $2.4M 'net ARR' headline, and no contribution figure is shown.
Slide 17: 'Not netted: the one-time $1.47M of engineering (14 of our 60 engineers for two quarters at $210,000 a year)'. The $2.4M headline ignores it, and there is no payback calculation.

Slides 16–17 net a $1.1M mobile-churn cost (57.6M × 14% × 27% × half a year, 'as if the rewrite would end all mobile churn') against the Pro launch. They cite 27% vs 6% churn and 38% vs 19% feature rank, and make locking the rewrite date and team a condition. No flip point is given for the share of churn the rewrite removes.

Slides 7–8 size the add-on from the paywall test (14%, about 1,372 accounts, $2.45M) against the survey's 46% and $8M. They flag the survey's 6% response and 9.4-seat bias, and call the paywall rate a ceiling because it comes from larger volunteer accounts. The headline Pro figure, though, uses the 33% precedent instead.

Slides 11 and 18 say inference is fixed at $0.009 only through December 2027 and that list prices fell 35%. All margin math uses $0.009 with no assumed price fall. The next steps include opening 2028 inference contract talks. The 'reprice before renewal' wording is vague.

Slide 9: 1,560 contested opportunities × 7 pp × $5,878 = about $0.6M a year, a ceiling. It cites 109 fewer wins and the 20% discount as a partial cause, and shows the VP Sales claim (328 recovered deals) exceeds the whole fall. This enters the slide 17 net.

alternatives.evidence: This is the recommendation: Pro at +$12 per seat with a 667 requests/seat allowance and request packs. It is supported by the 2023 precedent (33%, $2.9M), the 26% NRR threshold, margin scenarios (76% / 74.1% / 75.7%) and the Routewise match.

The flat $149 add-on is sized on the paywall test ($2.45M, $61.20 cost) and rejected. Its fixes (a lower entry price, or usage charges above an allowance) are not evaluated as an add-on. Request packs appear only inside Pro.
The document never evaluates delaying Copilot for two quarters and shipping the mobile rewrite first. It treats the rewrite delay as a cost to accept and does not compare it with the alternative.
There is no evaluation of bundling Copilot into Core at no charge with a hard cap, and no margin-floor test of that option.

sensitivities.evidence: The adoption drivers are shown: add-on 14% vs survey 46% ($2.45M vs $8M), Pro 33% ($2.9M), and the 26% Pro threshold for 4 NRR points. It does not show Pro results at lower uptake or the add-on's NRR threshold, nor does it apply the 14% selection-bias ceiling to Pro.

Slide 14 shows margin moving with usage: 76% at mean use, 74.1% at buyer-level use uncapped (below the floor), and 75.7% with the cap. Per-account costs run from $32.40 to $130.50. It gives no break-even request level and no margin sensitivity to the post-2027 per-request price.

The document gives dollar ceilings for both drivers: win-back at most $0.6M, with the discount named as part of the fall and the memo's 328 recovered deals refuted. Mobile-delay cost is at most $1.1M (38% of Pro ARR), stated as if the rewrite ended all mobile churn. It does not vary the AI-attributed share or give the mobile-churn share at which launching first becomes better.

overclaim.quote: The real cost is the two-quarter mobile delay, yet launching still adds about $2.4M of net ARR under five conditions (also slide 17: 'Even charging the mobile delay in full, launching in Pro adds about $2.4M of net ARR in the first year')

omissions: The $2.4M 'net ARR' mixes ARR with a churn estimate. It leaves out the $1.47M one-off engineering and the roughly $1.86M a year Copilot cost (inference + $0.6M run cost) against $2.89M Pro ARR. There is no contribution or payback view, so the headline overstates the first-year economics.

It pairs the maximum win-back ($0.6M) with the maximum mobile cost ($1.1M). It does not show the net range or the mobile-churn share at which launching first would be the better choice, and it does not compare delaying Copilot with launching (no delay alternative).

There is no downside case for Pro uptake. At the 14% seen in the paywall test (a ceiling), Pro would reach only about $1.2M, well below the $2.3M NRR need. The 'review Pro uptake after two quarters' condition names no threshold or trigger.
The cannibalisation risk that Core accounts who would not otherwise leave pay more, with price already the second churn reason (22%), is not examined.
unsupported_assumptions: 'Our 2023 higher tier drew 33% of accounts within a year; at that rate Pro adds about $2.9M of ARR': the headline $2.9M rests on a precedent that, as slide 13 admits, 'did not include AI', so Copilot's pull is untested.

'Pro inference cost assumes Pro accounts use Copilot like the mean beta account' (3,600 requests): the 76% margin depends on this. The mean comes from volunteer accounts, while the only paying evidence is 6,800 requests, where margin is 74.1% uncapped.
'Accounts that move have the average 6.2 seats': Pro ARR and cost both depend on this. Self-selecting movers are likely larger and heavier users.
'Allowance of 667 requests per seat a month': a working assumption chosen by the deck team, with no evidence on customer acceptance or on how it changes uptake or usage.
'Churn, contraction and other expansion stay at today's level, so Pro carries the whole gap': the NRR threshold of 26% depends on this.
